props.title: Shampoo

sections.content: **Shampoo** (1975) brilliantly captures the sunset of 1960s hedonism through the lens of a sexually adventurous Beverly Hills hairdresser. Set during Nixon's 1968 election, Warren Beatty's George is a fascinating precursor to the male protagonists we'd later see in **American Gigolo** (1980) and **American Psycho** (2000) - attractive professionals whose surface charm masks deeper emptiness. The film's genius lies in how it uses the hairdressing profession as both sexual metaphor and class commentary, predating similar explorations of beauty industry power dynamics in **Legally Blonde** (2001) and **Steel Magnolias** (1989).

sections.content: Director Hal Ashby, fresh off **Harold and Maude** (1971), brings his signature mix of satire and melancholy to the proceedings. The film's treatment of sexuality feels remarkably modern - neither prudish nor exploitative, it presents George's liaisons as both exciting and ultimately hollow. Julie Christie, Goldie Hawn, and Lee Grant (who won an Oscar) play fully realized characters rather than conquests, anticipating the complex female roles in later films like **Working Girl** (1988) and **9 to 5** (1980).

The political backdrop proves crucial - as Nixon's victory looms, the free-love optimism of the 60s gives way to the materialistic 70s. This cultural shift echoes through later films like **Boogie Nights** (1997) and **The Ice Storm** (1997), which similarly chronicle the dark side of sexual liberation. The script by Robert Towne and Warren Beatty masterfully weaves personal and political themes, much like Towne's work on **Chinatown** (1974). SUBHEAD: Sexual Politics and Social Commentary

sections.content: The film's treatment of class and power remains strikingly relevant. George's profession gives him intimate access to wealthy women's lives, yet he remains an outsider - a dynamic later explored in films like **Dinner at Eight** (1933) and **Gosford Park** (2001). His relationships with Goldie Hawn's Jill and Julie Christie's Jackie highlight the era's shifting sexual politics, while Lee Grant's Felicia represents the established order being upended.
